1.meaning: An oath sworn 'by the morning brightness' — the radiant forenoon light, the time after sunrise when the sun has climbed and its warmth spreads. Allah swears by this luminous part of the day to affirm the truth of what follows: that He has not abandoned His Prophet. The oath also evokes hope, warmth, and the return of light after darkness.
1.grammar: The 'wa' here is not 'and' but the particle of oath, meaning 'By…' — Allah is swearing an oath. An oath particle puts the noun after it into the genitive case, and that case ending belongs to the noun, not to the article 'al-'. The article 'al-' ('the') is invariable and never carries a case vowel. The noun ḍuḥā is a maqṣūr noun (one ending in alif maqṣūra, ى), so its final long 'ā' is fixed and does not change for case — there is no audible case ending at all on this word, whether nominative, accusative, or genitive. (Note on spelling: the long 'ā' written inside the word over the ح is a superscript/dagger-alif, ٰ, while the word-final 'ā' is written as the letter alif maqṣūra, ى — two different ways of writing the same long vowel.) Because ḍ is a 'sun letter,' the 'l' of al- assimilates into it, which is why the ض carries a shadda (ḍḍ) and you hear 'aḍ-ḍuḥā,' not 'al-ḍuḥā.'
1.root: ض-ح-و (ḍ-ḥ-w) — the forenoon, the brightness of the sun when it has risen high

1.meaning: An oath sworn by the night: 'and by the night.' The opening waw is the 'oath waw,' the same particle used to swear solemnly by a created thing as a sign pointing to its Maker. 'The night' here is the settled, deepening dark that follows the daytime brightness of the previous verse.
1.grammar: Three pieces fused into one word. The wa- is the 'waw of oath' ('by…'), which is why it forces the genitive case. al- is the definite article 'the.' The noun layl ('night') carries a final -i: that genitive ending is required because anything sworn by after the oath-waw is put in the genitive, exactly as English would mark it with 'by.'

2.meaning: 'When' — a particle that sets up a time clause pointing to a specific moment or condition: 'at the time when…' It links the oath to the precise circumstance described next, namely the night's growing still and dark.
2.grammar: An indeclinable particle of time, so it never changes its ending. It introduces the clause that follows and normally expects a verb after it (here sajā), giving the sense 'when it does such-and-such.' It typically carries a note of certainty about the event happening.

3.meaning: 'When it grows still / settles into darkness.' The verb describes the night as it spreads out, deepens, and becomes calm and silent — the hush of full nightfall when everything is enveloped and at rest.

parts.en: grew still / covered with calm dark (he/it)
(final root letter, surfacing as long ā)

3.grammar: A past-tense verb in the basic (form I) pattern, 3rd-person masculine singular ('it grew still'), agreeing with 'night' (a masculine noun). It takes no prefix. This is a defective (weak-final) verb whose third root letter is waw; in the 3rd-person masculine singular past, that final radical is written as alif maqsura (ٰى) and pronounced as a long -ā. Crucially, this -ā is the root's own final letter surfacing, not an added person/tense suffix — a sound (strong) verb in this very slot has a zero ending, with no vowel added after the last root consonant.
3.root: س-ج-و (s-j-w) — to be still, calm, and settled (of night growing dark and quiet)

1.meaning: A negation particle meaning "not." Placed before a past-tense verb here, it firmly denies that the action ever happened — "He did NOT do this." It rebuts the slander of the disbelievers who claimed the Prophet had been deserted.
1.grammar: This is a fixed particle with no endings to change — it never inflects. Standing in front of the past-tense verb that follows, it negates it outright: the deed simply did not occur. The tone is one of emphatic reassurance and denial.

2.meaning: To forsake, abandon, or take leave of someone and leave them behind. The intensive form here conveys a decisive, final parting — the very thing Allah is declaring He has NOT done to His Prophet.
2.grammar: This is a Form II verb (the doubled middle letter, -dd-, intensifies the basic sense of "parting" into a complete, deliberate forsaking). The bare -a ending on the stem is the past tense, "he did." The attached -ka is the object pronoun "you" (second-person masculine singular) — the one being (not) forsaken. Read with مَا before it: "He has not forsaken you."
2.root: و-د-ع (w-d-ʿ) — to leave, part from, bid farewell

3.meaning: Your Lord — the One who creates, owns, sustains, nurtures and governs you, bringing you step by step to completion. "Lord" only partly captures rabb, which fuses ownership, care and gradual upbringing into one word. The possessive "your" makes it tender and personal.
3.grammar: The -u ending is nominative: it flags rabb as the doer (subject) of the verb — it is your Lord who has not forsaken you. The attached -ka means "your" (second-person masculine singular), showing possession. Naming Him as "your Lord" rather than just "Allah" stresses His personal care for the Prophet.

4.meaning: "And not" — the linking word "and" joined to the negation particle "not," carrying the denial forward to a second statement: not only has He not forsaken you, neither has He done the next thing either.
4.grammar: Two fixed particles joined together, neither of which inflects. The wa- prefix simply means "and," connecting this clause to the one before. The mā again negates the past-tense verb that follows, so the reassurance is doubled: "...and He has not..."

5.meaning: To hate, to feel aversion or be angry with someone after once being close — to turn away in displeasure. Allah declares He has NOT done this to His Prophet: no anger, no aversion, no cooling of love.
5.grammar: A Form I past-tense verb, "he hated." The final -ā is the verb's own third root-letter (originally a weak letter written as a long "a"); it is not an added ending. The doer ("your Lord") is understood from the previous clause and is not repeated, and the object ("you") is left unstated for brevity and rhythm. With wamā before it: "nor has He become hateful of you."
5.root: ق-ل-ي / ق-ل-و (q-l-y) — to hate, loathe, turn away from

1.meaning: And surely the Hereafter — the next life, the eternal abode that follows this earthly existence. The word stacks three things onto one noun: 'and', an emphatic 'surely/certainly', and 'the', so it reads 'and most certainly the Hereafter'. In speech it is pronounced 'walalākhiratu' — the alif of 'the' drops out and the two lāms run together.

parts.en: the (article lām; its alif is elided here)

1.grammar: Two prefixes plus the article ride on one noun. 'wa-' is the connector 'and'. 'la-' is the prefixed lām of inception (lām al-ibtidāʾ): a lām attached to the front of a nominal sentence that adds emphasis, here reinforcing the oath, so it conveys 'surely/indeed'. Next comes the lām of the definite article 'the'; because it sits right after the emphatic lām, its alif is elided and only the consonant remains — hence the spoken form 'walal-' rather than a fully pronounced 'al-'. The stem 'ākhira' literally means 'the last/latter one' (feminine). The final '-u' (ḍamma) is the nominative ending, marking this word as the subject — 'the Hereafter [is]...' rather than the object.
1.root: ا-خ-ر (ʾ-kh-r) — to be last, to come after, the end

2.meaning: Better — greater in goodness and worth. Here it carries the comparative sense 'better (than)', and in Arabic this single form can also imply the superlative 'best'. It points to the Hereafter being superior to this present life for the Prophet.
2.grammar: This is the predicate — what is being said about the subject. 'khayr' is a special comparative word ('better/best') that does not take the usual 'afʿal' comparative pattern. The ending '-un' (two ḍammas, called tanwīn) is the nominative-indefinite marker: the doubled vowel signals 'a/an' (indefinite), and the nominative case fits its role as predicate, giving '[the Hereafter] is better'.
2.root: خ-ي-ر (kh-y-r) — goodness, to be good, to choose the better

3.meaning: For you — addressed specifically to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). It tells us in whose favour the Hereafter is better: it benefits and belongs to 'you'.
3.grammar: A two-piece word: the preposition 'li-' ('for/to') plus the suffix '-ka' ('you', singular masculine — the person being spoken to). The preposition's vowel here is fatḥa ('la-'), which is what 'li-' takes specifically before the attached second-person pronouns '-ka', '-ki', '-kum' and '-kunna'; before the pronouns '-hu', '-hā' and '-nā' it instead keeps its kasra (giving 'lahu', 'lahā', 'lanā'). So this fatḥa is not a universal rule for every attached pronoun. Together 'laka' = 'for you', and the '-ka' marks a single male addressee, here the Prophet.

4.meaning: Than — the comparison word that links 'better' to what it is being compared with. It introduces the thing surpassed: the Hereafter is better 'than' the first life.
4.grammar: This is the preposition 'min' ('from'), which after a comparative like 'khayr' means 'than'. Its normally silent ending takes a short '-a' (fatḥa) here purely to ease pronunciation into the following 'al-' ('the') — it is not a case ending, just a linking vowel so 'min al-' is read smoothly as 'mina l-'.

5.meaning: The first (life) — i.e. this present, earthly world, called 'the first' because it comes before the Hereafter. The noun 'life' is understood and not spoken; the feminine form agrees with the implied word 'al-ḥayāt' (the life).
5.grammar: 'al-' is 'the'; 'ūlā' is the feminine form of 'awwal' ('first'), agreeing with the unspoken feminine noun 'life'. Although it follows the preposition 'min' (which normally calls for the genitive), 'ūlā' belongs to a class of words whose ending never changes for case (it always ends in the fixed long vowel 'ā'), so no case-vowel is shown. In meaning it is genitive — 'than the first [life]'.
5.root: ا-و-ل (ʾ-w-l) — to be first, the beginning, foremost

1.meaning: A cluster of three small words fused into one: "and" + an emphasis particle that strengthens and confirms the promise ("truly, certainly") + a particle that points to the future ("will, is going to"). Together they mean roughly "and certainly, in time, He will surely..." — a solemn divine assurance of something yet to come.
1.grammar: Three prefixed particles, none of which take case endings. The wa- joins this verse to the oaths before it. The la- is the "lam of emphasis," which makes a statement sound like a sworn guarantee. sawfa is a future-tense marker placed before a verb to say the action WILL happen — and unlike the shorter sa-, sawfa carries a sense of a fuller, weightier "surely shall."

2.meaning: "He will give to you" — the act of granting, bestowing, and handing over a gift, here promising lavish future favour from Allah to the Prophet.
2.grammar: A present-future verb (form IV, the giving/causing-to-have pattern from the root). The yu- prefix marks a third-person masculine singular subject ("he"); driven by sawfa before it, the meaning is firmly future: "he will give." The final -ka is an attached object pronoun meaning "you" (masculine singular) — the one receiving the gift. The long -ī of yuʿṭī is the verb's own inherent stem vowel, present because its final root letter is a weak waaw (the stem yuʿṭī stands on its own, with or without a suffix). It is NOT a stretched-out form of the indicative -u ending; in fact, once the object pronoun -ka is attached, that -u mood marker simply drops away, leaving the stem's natural -ī before the pronoun.

3.meaning: "Your Lord" — rabb is a deeply loaded term: not merely a master but the One who creates, owns, sustains, nurtures, and brings to maturity. "Your Lord" frames Allah as the Prophet's own personal Cherisher and Caretaker, the source of the promised gift.
3.grammar: A noun followed by an attached possessive pronoun. The -u ending on rabb is nominative, marking it as the SUBJECT of the sentence — the doer of the giving (it is "your Lord" who will give). The attached -ka means "your" (masculine singular), forming a possessive link: "the Lord OF you / your Lord."

4.meaning: "...so that you will be well-pleased / fully content" — describing the Prophet reaching a state of complete satisfaction and joyful acceptance once the divine gift is granted.
4.grammar: The verb is present-tense: the ta- prefix marks a second-person masculine singular subject ("you"). It ends in a long final -ā (written with alif maqṣūra ـى), the natural ending of this verb whose root closes in a weak letter. The prefix fa- here is the "fa- of result" (fā' al-sabab), which presents this clause as the OUTCOME of the giving ("He will give... so that you become pleased") and puts the verb in the subjunctive mood (manṣūb). The future sense — "you WILL be pleased" — comes from this result-clause construction itself (fa- + subjunctive = "so that you will be pleased"); it is not governed by sawfa, whose scope reaches only the earlier verb yuʿṭīka.
4.root: ر-ض-و (r-ḍ-w) — to be pleased, content, satisfied

1.meaning: A two-part opening that turns a statement into a gentle rhetorical question: 'Did He not...?' It fuses the questioning particle a- ('did...?') with lam ('not'), which negates the past. Together they don't expect the answer 'no' — they invite the listener to affirm what follows: 'Did He not indeed find you...?' i.e. 'He surely did.'

parts.en: 'not' — a particle that negates and pushes the following verb into the past

1.grammar: This is a question built on a denial, used to affirm something the hearer already knows. The particle lam does two things to the verb that follows (yajid): it makes it mean the past ('did find') even though the verb wears a present-tense shape, and it puts that verb into the jussive mood — which is why the verb ends in a silent stop (-d, yajid) rather than a vowel. So the pair a- + lam = 'Did He not...?', a warm, rhetorical 'surely He did.'

2.meaning: 'He found you' — in the sense of 'He came upon you' or 'discovered you to be (in a certain state).' Here Allah is the one who found, and 'you' is the Prophet (peace be upon him). The verb sets up a description of the state he was found in: an orphan.

parts.en: 'you' (a single male) — the one who is found

2.grammar: The core yajid carries an unspoken 'he' as its subject — the prefix ya- marks a third-person masculine doer ('he'). Normally this shape is present tense ('he finds'), but because the particle lam from the previous word governs it, it shifts to past meaning ('he found') and to the jussive mood, which strips the final vowel and leaves the cut-off ending -d (yajid, not yajidu). The attached -ka is the object 'you' (masculine singular, accusative). So the whole = 'He found you.'
2.root: و-ج-د (w-j-d) — to find, to come upon, to discover

3.meaning: 'an orphan' — in classical usage, a child whose father has died (and, more broadly, one left without a parent's care). It describes the condition in which the Prophet (peace be upon him) was found: his father died before his birth, and his mother while he was still young. It points to vulnerability and need that Allah then answered.

parts.en: the '-an' ending: marks it as the object/description and signals 'a' (an orphan)

3.grammar: This is a noun acting as a complement describing the state of 'you' — 'He found you [being] an orphan.' The final -an ending (written as tanwīn, a doubled vowel sign) does two jobs: it is the accusative case, fitting because it describes the object of 'found,' and the -n sound marks the word as indefinite, i.e. 'an orphan' rather than 'the orphan.'

4.meaning: 'so He gave [you] shelter' — He took you in, provided refuge, and cared for you. The opening 'so/then' shows this as Allah's response to the need just mentioned: finding the Prophet (peace be upon him) an orphan, He sheltered him.

parts.en: 'so' / 'then' — links it as the result of what came before

4.grammar: The prefix fa- means 'so' or 'and then,' presenting this as the consequence: He found you an orphan, so He sheltered you. The verb āwā is a past-tense Form IV verb (the causative 'to give shelter') with a built-in 'He' as subject; its 'you' object (the Prophet, peace be upon him) is understood from the flow rather than spelled out. The final long -ā is how this verb's past-tense 'he' form ends, since its last root letter is a weak vowel — giving āwā = 'He sheltered.'
4.root: ء-و-ي (ʾ-w-y) — to take in, to give shelter or refuge

1.meaning: "And He found you" — the verb describes Allah finding or encountering the Prophet in a particular condition; the attached "you" is the Prophet himself, the object being found.
1.grammar: The opening وَ (wa) is the connector "and," tying this favour to the ones before it. وَجَدَ (wajada) is a past-tense verb in the third-person masculine singular — the bare stem with the built-in "he" subject (Allah). The final ـكَ (-ka) is an attached object pronoun, "you" (masculine singular), so the whole reads "and He found you."
1.root: و-ج-د (w-j-d) — to find, to come upon, to perceive

2.meaning: "Lost / astray" — describing the Prophet as one who had not yet been given the light of revelation: unaware of the Book and faith, seeking but not yet guided. It is not sin but a state of not-yet-knowing the way.

parts.en: lost, straying, not finding the way
accusative ending (marks it as the object describing 'you')

2.grammar: This is an active participle ("one who is straying / lost") functioning as the description of "you" — i.e., it tells us the condition Allah found him in. The final ـًا (-an, the tanwīn fatḥa) is the accusative indefinite ending: it marks the word as the second object describing the one who was found ("He found you [being] lost"). Note: the source splits this word, placing only ضَآ under this index and the rest under the next, but the transliteration ḍāllan shows it is the single word ضَآلًّا.
2.root: ض-ل-ل (ḍ-l-l) — to go astray, to lose one's way

3.meaning: "So He guided" — Allah then gave guidance: He showed the way, sending down revelation and faith so that the Prophet was no longer without direction. The opening "so/then" marks this as the response to the previous state.
3.grammar: The prefix فَ (fa) means "so" or "then," showing result and sequence — the guiding follows from the finding. هَدٰى (hadā) is a past-tense verb, third-person masculine singular ("he guided," subject Allah). Its ending is the long ـٰى (-ā), the verb's natural final vowel for this weak-ending root; the object "you" is understood from context ("He guided [you]"). Note: the source attaches the stray fragment لًّا (the tail of the previous word ḍāllan) to this index, but the transliteration fahadā confirms the actual word here is فَهَدٰى.
3.root: ه-د-ي (h-d-y) — to guide, to lead rightly, to show the way

1.meaning: And He found you — Allah found, came upon, or discovered you (the Prophet, peace be upon him) in a particular state. This clause continues the list of past favours that the surah recalls: the rhetorical question 'Did He not find you...?' opens earlier (in ayah 6), and this phrase carries that same force forward with 'and'.
1.grammar: Three pieces. The wa- prefix is the connective 'and', linking this to the previous favours mentioned. The core is a past-tense verb 'wajada' (He found): the bare stem with the final -a vowel marks it as third-person masculine singular past — 'He did find' — with Allah as the unstated subject. The attached -ka on the end is the object 'you' (addressing one male), so the whole reads 'And He found you'.
1.root: و-ج-د (w-j-d) — to find, to come upon, to discover

2.meaning: In need / poor — describing the Prophet (peace be upon him) as one who was in straitened circumstances, lacking wealth and having dependents to support. It paints the picture of someone financially needy before Allah provided for him.
2.grammar: This is an active participle ('one who is X') built on the pattern fāʿil from the verb ʿāla, 'to be poor / to have a family to provide for'. The final -an ending (the 'tanwīn' double-fatḥa) does two jobs at once: it marks the word as indefinite ('a needy one') and puts it in the accusative case, because it is the description of the 'you' that He found — 'He found you [being] needy'.
2.root: ع-ي-ل (ʿ-y-l) — to be in want, to have dependents to support

3.meaning: So He made you self-sufficient / free of need — Allah enriched you and made you independent of others, removing the earlier poverty. The sense is being made content and provided for, not merely given cash, so that one no longer needs to depend on anyone but Allah.

parts.en: He enriched / made free of need

3.grammar: Two pieces. The fa- prefix means 'so' or 'then', showing the result that followed: He found you needy, SO He enriched you. The core 'aghnā' is a past-tense verb in Form IV (the af'ala pattern, formed with a prefixed hamza): this is the causative form, so it does not mean merely 'to be rich' (ghaniya) but 'to MAKE someone rich / free of need'. It is third-person masculine singular past ('He did enrich'), with Allah as the subject; the final long -ā is the verb's weak last root-letter, the normal ending for such verbs.
3.root: غ-ن-ي (gh-n-y) — to be free of need, rich, self-sufficient

1.meaning: A two-part opener meaning roughly 'So, as for…'. It picks up the train of thought from the previous verses (where Allah recalled His favours) and turns to a command, singling out a specific case — 'now, regarding the orphan…' — and setting up the instruction that follows.

parts.en: so / and so (links to what came before)

1.grammar: Two joined particles. The prefix fa- is a connector meaning 'so/then', drawing a consequence from the earlier verses. ammā is a detailing particle that isolates a topic ('as for X…') and normally pairs with a fa- later in the sentence before the answer — here that partner is the fa- on word 3 (falā). Particles like these do not change for case or tense; they have fixed forms.

2.meaning: The orphan — a child whose father has died, left without a protector. The verse echoes the Prophet's own early life as an orphan, so the term carries the weight of someone vulnerable and deserving of compassion.
2.grammar: The prefix al- is 'the', making it definite ('the orphan'). The final -a vowel (yatīm-a) is the accusative case: the word is the direct object (maf'ūl bihi) of the verb 'do not oppress' (taqhar) further on, brought forward ahead of it. So the case ending points to that verb. The transliteration shows it as 'l-yatīma' rather than 'al-yatīma' because the helping vowel at the start of al- (the hamzat al-wasl) drops out after the preceding vowel — the final -ā of ammā runs straight into the l-. The lam itself is fully pronounced: ya' (ي) is a moon letter, so there is no assimilation of the l- into the following sound.

3.meaning: A two-part phrase meaning 'then do not…'. It delivers the response to 'as for the orphan' and introduces a prohibition — telling the listener what not to do.
3.grammar: The prefix fa- is the answering connector that completes the 'as for the orphan…' structure begun by ammā in word 1 ('as for the orphan, THEN…'). lā here is the lā of prohibition — a command meaning 'do not', which puts the following verb into the jussive (command) form. Both are unchanging particles.

4.meaning: Do not crush, subdue, or treat harshly. The verb means to overpower someone weaker — to bully, dominate, or wrong them. Combined with the preceding 'do not', it is a direct command: never deal oppressively with the orphan.
4.grammar: A present-tense verb in the form-I pattern, with the ta- prefix marking 'you' (singular, addressed to the Prophet and every listener). Because it follows the prohibition lā, it takes the jussive ending — shown by the bare final consonant (taqhar, with no added vowel) — which turns 'you oppress' into the command 'do not oppress'.
4.root: ق-ه-ر (q-h-r) — to overpower, subdue, dominate by force

1.meaning: A two-part connector that turns attention to a new case: 'and as for...' / 'and as regards...'. It singles out a topic (here, the one who asks) and sets up the instruction that will follow about how to treat him. It pairs with the 'fa-' ('then') on a later word to form the structure 'as for X... then [do this].'
1.grammar: Two particles joined together. 'wa-' is the simple joiner 'and.' 'ammā' is a detailing/conditional particle meaning 'as for'; it lifts up a topic for special comment and normally requires a matching 'fa-' ('then/so') in front of the reply clause — which we get in word 3 (falā). There is no case ending to read here; these are invariable particles that do not change form.

2.meaning: The one who asks — a person making a request. It covers both the beggar asking for material help and the seeker asking for knowledge or guidance; classical commentators read it broadly to include anyone who comes to you in need and puts a request to you.
2.grammar: An active participle ('the one who is asking') built on the doer-pattern fāʿil, carrying the definite article 'al-' ('the'). The 'l' of 'al-' assimilates into the following sun-letter 's', which is why it is pronounced 'as-sāil' with a doubled s (shown by the shaddah on the sīn). The final '-a' is the accusative ending. This word is the fronted object (maf'ul bihi muqaddam) of the verb in word 4: the 'ammā... fa-' frame pulls the object out of its normal place after the verb and sets it up first as the topic of the clause, so the sense is 'as for the asker, then do not repel [him].' It is accusative precisely because it is still the grammatical object of 'tanhar' even though it has been moved to the front of the topicalization frame.
2.root: س-أ-ل (s-ʾ-l) — to ask, to request, to beg

3.meaning: 'then do not...' — the hinge that delivers the actual command after the topic has been raised. The 'then' answers the earlier 'as for...,' and the 'not' makes what follows a prohibition.
3.grammar: Two particles. 'fa-' ('then/so') is the required response-marker that completes the 'as for...' opening of word 1. 'lā' here is the 'lā' of prohibition: placed before a present-tense verb it turns it into a negative command ('do not do it'), and it puts that verb into the jussive mood — which is why the verb's ending is clipped (see word 4). No case ending applies to particles.

4.meaning: Do not drive him away, scold him, or rebuff him harshly. The verb means to repel someone with a sharp, demeaning rejection; the instruction is to refuse, if you must refuse, gently and never to crush or humiliate the one who asks.
4.grammar: A present-tense verb addressed to a single male 'you' — the 'ta-' prefix marks the second-person masculine singular subject ('you'); the corresponding 'he' form would instead take a 'ya-' prefix (yanhar). Under the prohibition word 'lā' (word 3) the verb stands in the jussive mood, which strips the ending down to a bare, vowelless stop ('tanhar' rather than 'tanharu'); that clipped ending is the grammatical sign that this is a command not to act. Built on the simple Form I pattern, so it carries the plain, basic sense of the root.
4.root: ن-ه-ر (n-h-r) — to rebuke, to repel, to drive away harshly

1.meaning: A two-part opening best read as 'And as for...'. The 'wa' is a connector ('and') joining this verse to the two parallel clauses before it (about the orphan and the one who asks), while 'ammā' is a framing particle that singles out a new topic to comment on. It sets up an 'as for X, then do Y' structure, here leading into the command at the end of the verse.

parts.en: as for / when it comes to

1.grammar: 'wa' is a simple joining word ('and'). 'ammā' is a particle of detail and condition meaning 'as for'; it raises a subject and demands a follow-up clause that begins with 'fa-' ('then'), which arrives on the final word 'faḥaddith'. It has no case ending — it is a fixed particle, not a noun or verb.
1.root: — (particles: wa = 'and'; ammā = topic/detail marker — no triliteral root)

2.meaning: 'With the blessing/favour of...'. The core word niʿma denotes a divine grace, gift, or favour bestowed by Allah — every good thing one has been granted. The attached 'bi-' ('with/about') ties it to the closing command: the favour is what one is to speak about and make known.

parts.en: feminine ending, here in the genitive (-i)

2.grammar: 'bi-' is a prefixed preposition ('with/about'), and any noun after it must take the genitive case — which is why the word ends in '-i' (niʿma-ti). The 'ta marbūta' (ة) is the feminine noun ending, pronounced '-t-' here because the word is joined to what follows. This noun is also the first term (muḍāf) of a possessive chain (iḍāfa) with the next word: 'the favour OF...'.

3.meaning: 'Your Lord'. Rabb is far richer than 'master' or 'lord': it means the One who creates, owns, sustains, nurtures and brings to maturity — the Cherisher who provides for and governs all of one's affairs. The attached '-ka' makes it personal and singular: 'your Lord', addressed to the Prophet (and through him, each believer).
3.grammar: 'rabb' carries the genitive '-i' (rabb-i) because it is the second term (muḍāf ilayhi) of the possessive chain begun by the previous word — 'the favour OF your Lord'. The attached '-ka' is the possessive pronoun 'your' for a single male addressee. Together they read 'your Lord', and the whole phrase means 'the blessing of your Lord'.
3.root: ر-ب-ب (r-b-b) — to nurture, sustain, master, bring up

4.meaning: 'Then speak about it / proclaim it!'. A command to talk openly about the favour just mentioned — to mention, relate and make Allah's blessing known to others, as an act of gratitude rather than concealing it.
4.grammar: 'fa-' means 'then/so' and is the required answer (apodosis link) to the 'ammā' ('as for') opening — it completes the 'as for X, then do Y' frame. 'ḥaddith' is a command (imperative) addressed to one male: 'do speak / proclaim!'. Its silent ending (no final vowel, marked sukūn) is exactly what an imperative takes. It is Form II of the root, an intensive 'make-it-happen' pattern: not just 'to be told' but 'to actively tell, relate and broadcast'.
4.root: ح-د-ث (ḥ-d-th) — to relate, narrate, speak of something new
